498.title: Vishvamitra asks for Rama
498.hook: a king promises a sage anything, then hears what he wants
498.howItsDone: Vishvamitra is honored in Hindu tradition as one of the great rishis; the Gayatri mantra of the Rig Veda is traditionally credited to him, and his request for Rama is told as the moment the prince's life of service begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dasharatha's sacrifice bore fruit: four sons from the fire, born to answer Ravana's boast. Your line: avatar, God comes down as one of us.
screen: `AVATAR: GOD COMES DOWN AS ONE OF US.`

segments.voice: The four princes grow up learned, brave and close. Lakshmana sticks to Rama like a second shadow; Shatrughna to Bharata. Dasharatha, delighted, is already talking with his counselors about their weddings. Then a guard rushes in: the sage Vishvamitra is at the gate. Dasharatha hurries out, washes his feet, honors him, and says the words a king says to an honored guest, and maybe shouldn't: whatever you ask, consider it done. Vishvamitra smiles, and asks.
screen: `FOUR PRINCES, GROWN.` → `A FAMOUS SAGE AT THE GATE.` → `WHATEVER YOU ASK, IT'S DONE.`

segments.voice: Vishvamitra explains. He's begun a sacrifice, and two rakshasas, Maricha and Subahu, keep wrecking it, pouring blood and flesh on the altar. Under his vow he can't curse them in anger. So he asks for Rama. Give me your eldest son, the boy who still wears a child's side-locks, for ten nights, to guard my rite. Dasharatha's world tilts. He pleads, and Valmiki gives us his words: unashodasha-varsho me ramo rajivalochanah. My lotus-eyed Rama is not yet sixteen. He's never fought. Take my army instead. Take me. And when he hears who stands behind those two rakshasas, Ravana, he grows more frightened still. No, not Rama. Now, Vishvamitra was born a king, and became a sage of the highest rank through fierce austerity. His name means friend of the whole world, but when a promise is taken back, his fire rises. You're breaking your word, king, he says. Fine. I'll go as I came. And the whole earth, the text says, trembles. Why would the earth shake over one sentence? Because in Hinduism a word given is satya, truth, and Hindu texts name truthfulness again and again as part of dharma, the order that holds the world together. A much later retelling in Awadhi, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, sums up the rule of Rama's family: life may go, but the word must not. So Dasharatha stands between two things his tradition takes seriously: satya, and a father's love. The text doesn't call his fear wrong. Tomorrow, someone helps him choose.
screen: `TWO RAKSHASAS RUIN HIS SACRIFICE.` · `RAMA IS NOT YET SIXTEEN.` · `YOU'RE BREAKING YOUR WORD.` · `THE EARTH TREMBLES.` · then, large: `A GIVEN WORD IS SATYA.`

segments.voice: Before a puja or a vow, many Hindus make a sankalpa: they say plainly what they intend to do. Try a small one. Think of one promise you've made that has gotten heavier, to a child, a friend, yourself. On the breath in, say it to yourself once, simply, the way a king's word was said at the gate. On the breath out, ask: can I keep it, and what would help? If you pray, offer it to God as a word you mean to keep. If you don't, just hold it honestly.
Vishvamitra, friend of the whole world. The king-turned-sage asks Dasharatha for Rama, and a father's love meets a king's given word.
Your line: a given word is satya. A father's fear, and a promise that shook the earth. See you tomorrow.

499.title: The dawn verse
499.hook: the verse that wakes Rama on his first morning away from home is still sung at dawn
499.carry: pray at sandhya, where night meets day
499.howItsDone: The Venkatesha Suprabhatam, sung at dawn at the Tirumala temple and played in many homes, opens with Vishvamitra's verse from the Bala Kanda waking Rama.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vishvamitra asked for Rama, a father pleaded, and the earth shook at a broken promise. Your line was a given word is satya.

In many homes and temples in South India, the day starts with a recording of a Sanskrit hymn, the Venkatesha Suprabhatam, a song to wake the Lord at Tirupati. Its very first verse isn't new. It's borrowed, word for word, from the Ramayana: what Vishvamitra says to wake Rama on his first morning away from home, sleeping on grass by a river. But first, the boys have to leave.
screen: `A HYMN AT DAWN IN SOUTH INDIA.` → `ITS FIRST VERSE IS FROM THE RAMAYANA.` → `RAMA'S FIRST MORNING AWAY.`

segments.voice: Vasishtha, the royal priest, speaks to the frightened king. You've given your word, he says. Breaking it would undo all your merit. And Vishvamitra knows every divine weapon there is; Rama will be safer with him than anywhere. Dasharatha yields, and keeps his word. He calls for Rama, and Lakshmana, who won't be left behind, and blesses them. The boys walk out after the sage, bows in hand, and the text says a soft breeze blew and flowers fell from the sky. On the south bank of the Sarayu, Vishvamitra teaches Rama two mantras, bala and atibala, strength and great strength: with these, he says, you won't feel hunger or thirst or tiredness. That night the princes sleep on grass, like ordinary travelers. At dawn the sage wakes them: kausalya supraja rama purva sandhya pravartate, uttishtha narashardula kartavyam daivam ahnikam. Rama, fortunate son of Kausalya, the dawn twilight is here. Rise, tiger among men; the day's sacred duties are waiting. The boys rise, bathe and say their prayers before they walk on. Listen to the word in the middle of that verse: sandhya, the meeting point of night and day. Hindus have long treated these junctions, dawn and dusk above all, as times to turn to God; the daily prayer at them is called sandhya-vandana, honoring the twilight. That's why the verse still works. Every morning at Tirupati, the temple wakes the Lord with the words a sage used to wake a prince, and many homes wake with him.

segments.voice: Try what the boys did at sandhya: before the phone, before the news, turn first toward the sacred. Sit facing the light if you can. Breathe in: the night is done. Breathe out: the day's duties are waiting, and they can wait one more breath. If you pray, say one line to God, a name, a verse, the start of the Suprabhatam if you know it. If you don't, simply greet the day before it starts asking things of you.

500.title: Tataka's forest
500.hook: a forest that used to be farmland, and the story of who emptied it
500.howItsDone: Tataka's story is told in Ramayana recitations and in Ramlila performances as the young Rama's first test; some teachers pause on Rama's question and Vishvamitra's answer, since Hindu learning has long been carried on by question and answer between student and guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the boys left home, learned bala and atibala, and woke to a sage's dawn verse. Your line was pray at sandhya, where night meets day. And today's number is worth a pause: five hundred days.

The three travelers cross the Ganga where the Sarayu pours into it, and Rama hears the roar of the two rivers meeting. On the far side, the land changes. A dark, thick forest. No paths. Crickets, harsh birdcalls, lions, tigers, boars, elephants. Nobody lives here. What is this place, Rama asks. The sage's answer surprises him. Not long ago, these were two rich farming lands, full of people and harvests. Someone emptied them.
screen: `WHERE TWO RIVERS MEET.` → `A FOREST WITH NO PATHS.` → `IT USED TO BE FARMLAND.`

segments.voice: Her name is Tataka. She was born a yakshi, a nature spirit, daughter of a yaksha named Suketu, who prayed for a child and was given a daughter with the strength of a thousand elephants. She married Sunda and had a son, Maricha: the same Maricha who has been ruining Vishvamitra's sacrifice. When her husband died, Tataka and her son attacked the great sage Agastya, and Agastya cursed them both. Maricha became a rakshasa. Tataka became a terrible devourer, and since then she has turned this whole country into wilderness. She has to be stopped, the sage says. By you. Rama stops. Valmiki lets him ask a real question: she's a woman; how can a woman have such strength? The sage, knowing what Rama is really asking, makes his case before Rama acts. A protector has a duty. When anyone, man or woman, is destroying the lives of others, the protector cannot step back. It's a hard teaching, and the text doesn't hide that it's hard. But notice what Valmiki honors first: the question. Hindu learning has always run on questions. The Upanishads are mostly conversations, a student asking, a teacher answering. And the Bhagavad Gita says the way to learn is by bowing to the teacher, by asking, and by serving. Rama does all three. He trusts his guru enough to ask, and his guru respects him enough to answer before asking him to act. Tomorrow, what he decides.
screen: `FARMLAND TURNED TO WILDERNESS.` · `A YAKSHI, CURSED BY AGASTYA.` · `RAMA STOPS AND ASKS.` · `LEARN BY BOWING, ASKING, SERVING.` · then, large: `TĀṬAKĀ.`

segments.voice: Five hundred days; let that land for a breath. Then bring one real question to the sit: something about God, your path, or a teaching that has never sat right with you. Don't rush to answer it. Hold it honestly, the way Rama held his before he acted. If you pray, offer the question itself as the prayer. If you don't, just let it be asked. In this tradition, asking is part of the path.

Your line: ask the guru, then act. Rama questioned first, and his teacher answered. Day five hundred, and counting.

501.title: Rama and Tataka
501.hook: Rama decides, and tries the gentlest way first
501.carry: ahimsa comes first, force only to protect
501.howItsDone: In Ramayana recitation and performance, Tataka's defeat is told as Rama's first act of protecting the land; commentators and modern readers discuss it in different ways, and some draw attention to Rama's reluctance, reading it alongside ahimsa, the Hindu value of not harming.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a forest that used to be farmland, a yakshi under a curse, and Rama's real question. Your line was ask the guru, then act.

Rama has listened, and his answer isn't a simple yes. My father told me to do whatever you say, he tells the sage. So I'll do this, for the sake of the cows, the sages and the land. He's acting from obedience, from a promise, not from appetite for a fight. Then he lifts his bow and twangs the string. The sound rolls through the forest. And from deep in the trees, something hears it and comes running.
screen: `MY FATHER TOLD ME TO OBEY YOU.` → `THE TWANG OF THE BOWSTRING.` → `SOMETHING COMES RUNNING.`

segments.voice: Tataka charges out, raising clouds of dust, hurling rocks. Valmiki slows down here. Rama doesn't try to kill her. I'll just take away her power to harm, he tells Lakshmana; I don't want to take her life. He shoots and cuts off her arms. Lakshmana wounds her face. That should end it. It doesn't. Tataka uses her magic, turns invisible, changes shape, and rains stones on them from the air. Enough mercy, Rama, Vishvamitra calls. Evening is coming, and at dusk rakshasas grow stronger. So Rama, tracking her by sound, looses an arrow, and Tataka falls. The gods praise Rama, Vishvamitra embraces him, and the forest, the text says, is freed and becomes beautiful again. How do people read this scene? Traditional teachers see Rama's first act of protection, a land given back to its people, and point to how hard he tried not to kill. Some modern readers find it painful, a young man pressed to kill a woman, and read it with that discomfort in view. Both readings take the text seriously. Underneath both is a tension Hinduism lives with honestly. Ahimsa, not harming, is among its highest values. And a protector has a duty to stop those who are harming others. The Ramayana shows the order Rama keeps. He asked first. He obeyed a promise. He tried to disarm before he destroyed. Force came last, and only to protect.

segments.voice: Ahimsa starts small. Think of a situation where you have to be firm with someone, or will have to, and hold one question with the breath: what is the least harm that still protects the people who need protecting? Don't plan the whole conversation; let the gentlest step that would actually work come into view, and rest with it. If you pray, ask for the strength to be both firm and kind.

502.title: The gift of the astras
502.hook: the morning after the forest is freed, the sage hands over everything he has
502.carry: the guru gives mantras to the ready
502.howItsDone: In the epics, astras are given by teachers or gods to those judged worthy, invoked by mantra; in the same way, Hindu families and teachers traditionally hand on a mantra, such as the Gayatri at the sacred-thread ceremony, when the student is ready.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama obeyed a promise, tried to ahimsa comes first, force only to protect, and the forest was freed. Your line was ahimsa comes first, force only to protect.

They spend the night in the freed forest. In the morning, Vishvamitra is smiling. He has watched this boy ask before acting, obey without sulking, try mercy before force. Now the sage decides to hand over everything he has. Not land, not gold. Something no treasury holds, and no army could take from him. Sit down, he tells Rama, and get ready.
screen: `THE SAGE HAS BEEN WATCHING.` → `MERCY BEFORE FORCE.` → `NOW, EVERYTHING HE HAS.`

segments.voice: What Vishvamitra gives are the astras, the divine weapons. An astra isn't just an arrow. It's a power called up by a mantra and released through a weapon: the force of a god, carried on a word. The sage names them one after another, and the list runs on for verses. The discus of dharma and the discus of time. Indra's thunderbolt. The weapon of Brahma himself. The noose of Varuna, lord of the waters. The fire weapon, the wind weapon, and one called manava, named for Manu, the first human. As he recites, the weapons appear, not as metal but as shining beings, standing before Rama with palms joined. We are yours, they say. Tell us what to do. Rama touches each one and answers simply: stay in my mind, and come when I need you. And look when they're given. Not on day one, but after a test, once the sage has seen how this young man uses force. Hindu tradition still keeps this pattern. A mantra is traditionally received from a teacher, often at an initiation, when the teacher judges the student ready; that readiness is called adhikara. In many families, a boy's sacred-thread ceremony is when he's first given the Gayatri mantra, and the Gayatri is traditionally credited to Vishvamitra himself. The power waits for the person. It doesn't come first.
screen: `AN ASTRA: A GOD'S POWER ON A WORD.` · `THE WEAPONS APPEAR, PALMS JOINED.` · `GIVEN AFTER THE TEST.` · `ADHIKARA: READY TO RECEIVE.` · then, large: `STAY IN MY MIND.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus keep one mantra close: a name of God or a line received from a teacher or a parent, repeated quietly, a practice called japa. Sit, and repeat silently one sacred word you were given: Om, a name, a line your family says. If you don't have one, let the breath itself be the word. Don't send it anywhere. Ask it, the way Rama asked his, to stay in your mind and come when it's truly needed.

503.title: Calling the weapons back
503.hook: a young man with the gods' weapons asks the one question that matters next
503.carry: the wise know samhara, the calling back
503.howItsDone: Traditional teachers often point to Rama's request for the withdrawals of the weapons as a sign of his character, and the Gita's image of the tortoise drawing in its limbs uses the same word for self-mastery.

segments.voice: Yesterday: divine powers stood before Rama as shining beings, and he asked them to stay in his mind. Your line was the guru gives mantras to the ready.
screen: `THE GURU GIVES MANTRAS TO THE READY.`

segments.voice: Hand someone the keys to something enormous and listen to their first question. A new driver with a fast car. A new manager with the power to fire people. An eighteen-year-old with a credit card. It's nearly always: what can this do? How fast, how far, how much? Rama has just been handed the weapons of the gods. And walking on through the forest, he asks Vishvamitra something quieter, and wiser.
screen: `THE KEYS TO SOMETHING ENORMOUS.` → `THE USUAL QUESTION: WHAT CAN IT DO?` → `RAMA ASKS ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: I've received the weapons, Rama says, and even the gods would find them hard to overcome. Now teach me how to call them back. In Sanskrit, the release is prayoga; the withdrawal is samhara. Vishvamitra is delighted, and teaches him. Again the powers appear, a new company of shining beings, palms joined. These are the withdrawals: the knowledge of how to stop what you've started. Why does Valmiki give this a whole moment? Because in the epics a weapon you can't call back is a disaster. Rama, this young, asks for the brake before he ever touches the accelerator. And the same word comes back in the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna describes a person of steady wisdom as someone who can draw the senses back from what pulls at them, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs: yada samharate, when he withdraws. Samhara, again. That's a Hindu idea of strength. Not only what you can unleash, but what you can call back: a word, an appetite, a temper. The road goes on to a green hermitage on a hill, with deer grazing. This is Siddhashrama, the sage says, where Vishnu once did his austerities, the hermitage of Vamana, who asked King Bali for three steps of land and crossed the worlds in three strides. My sacrifice is waiting here. And here the weapons will be needed.
screen: `TEACH ME TO CALL THEM BACK.` · `PRAYOGA AND SAMHARA.` · `THE GITA: YADĀ SAṂHARATE CĀYAṂ KŪRMO 'ṄGĀNĪVA SARVAŚAḤ.` · `SIDDHASHRAMA, WHERE VAMANA LIVED.` · then, large: `SAṂHĀRA: THE WITHDRAWAL.`

segments.voice: Sit like the Gita's tortoise. Let attention come in from the world one sense at a time: the eyes soften, then the ears, then the busy hands go still. Every breath has a release and a return. Then think of one thing you set loose today, a mood, a comment, a scroll that ran too long, and practice calling it back, the way a breath comes home. If you pray, ask for that kind of strength.
The weapons. Rama asks not only how to release them but how to withdraw them, and Vishvamitra teaches him the samhara, the calling back.

504.title: The fire at Siddhashrama
504.hook: two boys stay awake six nights so a sacred fire can be finished
504.carry: guard the yajna, the sacred fire
504.howItsDone: The yajna Rama guards is the fire offering at the heart of Vedic worship; Hindus still offer into a sacred fire in the havan or homa at housewarmings and rites of passage, and circle it at weddings. Ramayana tellings also mark Maricha's survival here, since he returns in the Aranya Kanda as the golden deer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama asked how to call the weapons back, and the sage taught him the withdrawal. Your line was the wise know samhara, the calling back.

At Siddhashrama, Vishvamitra begins his sacrifice and takes a vow of silence; from now on he can't say a word. So the hermits tell the boys: for six days and six nights, you have to guard him. Rama and Lakshmana stand watch, bows ready, and don't sleep. Five days pass. Nothing. On the sixth, the altar fire suddenly flares up on its own. The sky goes dark. And out of the dark comes a roar, and a rain of blood.
screen: `A VOW OF SILENCE.` → `SIX NIGHTS ON WATCH.` → `THE SIXTH DAY: A RAIN OF BLOOD.`

segments.voice: Maricha and Subahu have come, with their followers, to wreck the rite. Rama takes up the manava weapon, the one named for Manu, the first human, and fires it at Maricha's chest. It doesn't kill him. It hurls him a hundred yojanas, far out over the sea, where he falls, stunned but alive. Then the fire weapon for Subahu, who falls dead, and the wind weapon for the rest. The sacrifice is finished. Vishvamitra, his vow complete, says: you've made the name of this place come true. Siddhashrama, the hermitage of accomplishment. Why does a whole week build toward guarding one fire? Because the yajna, the fire offering, is worship as old as Hinduism's oldest scriptures, the Vedas. In the Vedas, Agni, the fire, carries what's offered to the gods. Hindus still light that fire: a havan or homa at a housewarming, at a child's rites of passage, and at weddings, where the couple walks around the sacred fire. Rama spent six nights awake so one could be finished. Hold onto Maricha. He's still out there, and he'll come back as a golden deer. Now the week, from the top. A given word. A dawn verse. A question asked before acting. Ahimsa first, force last. Mantras given to the ready, and the strength to call them back. And today, the fire kept.
screen: `THE MANAVA FOR MARICHA.` · `HURLED OVER THE SEA, STILL ALIVE.` · `YAJNA: THE FIRE OFFERING.` · `HINDUS STILL LIGHT THAT FIRE.` · then, large: `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.`

segments.voice: Many Hindu homes light a small lamp, a diya, morning or evening, a small everyday flame offered to God. Light one if you can, or picture its flame. Then sit as if you're on watch, not tense, just awake: eyes low, back long, breath even, noticing each sound arrive and pass the way the boys watched the dark for six nights. If your attention wanders, come back to the flame without scolding yourself. If you pray, offer the sit itself.
The weapons. At Siddhashrama, Rama uses them for the first time: the manava hurls Maricha out to sea alive, and the yajna is completed.
Your line: guard the yajna, the sacred fire. Six nights awake, and the offering was finished. A week on the road, complete.
